newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Chirac's Middle East quest more pain than gain.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's Middle East quest more pain than gain.

text.p: In the holy city of Jerusalem, it is tempting to compare French President Jacques Chirac's quest for a bigger European role in Middle East peacemaking to the stations of the cross.

Chirac's shouting match with overzealous Israeli security men on the Via Dolorosa, the Old City street where Christians believe Jesus carried his cross to the crucifixion, dramatised Israel's hostility to his message -- that without a Palestinian state, the Jewish state will have no lasting security.
"I'm not sure it isn't more pain than gain here," the French leader quipped in a late-night aside.

Chirac himself pulled no punches on his two-day visit to Israel, the second and most difficult leg of a week-long Middle East tour, leaving analysts wondering whether he had deliberately courted confrontation, and why.

Grandstanding in Jerusalem may make him a hero in the Arab world, where France has important commercial interests and political ties, but it may not make Europe a credible co-sponsor of Arab-Israeli peace talks -- Chirac's avowed aim.

"This will just confirm many Israelis in their view that France is biased against Israel and cannot be an honest broker in the Middle East," said Yitzhak Minerbi, a former Israeli ambassador to the European Union.

While the French leader was venting anger at heavy-handed Israeli security in Arab East Jerusalem, U.S. envoy Dennis Ross was quietly mediating between the Israelis and the PLO on an Israeli troop pullout from the West Bank city of Hebron.
Chirac told a joint news conference with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu: "My only ambition in this region is to be a soldier of peace."
But Israel has made clear it would prefer U.S. mediation for the moment, although European funds to boost the Palestinian economy were welcome.

In a key speech on Monday, Chirac told Israelis that only a Palestinian state could guarantee their security and they would have to hand back the occupied Golan Heights to Syria and evacuate their troops from south Lebanon to win lasting peace.
Netanyahu, elected on a platform rejecting any further territorial concession and branding a Palestinian state a mortal threat to Israel, chose to stress the positive, calling Chirac a dear friend.
"Obviously we very much value the readiness of France to try to help us in the effort we are making...in the end to renew the bilateral negotiations between us and Syria," he said.
Their personal relations seemed genuinely warm and Netanyahu said Chirac had brought a positive message from his talks with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad.

But President Ezer Weizman used a toast on Monday night to slam the European Union, and especially France, for what he called their indulgent attitude towards Iran's ruling ayatollahs and Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
And Netanyahu effectively shot down an EU mediating role even before Chirac had touched down in Tel Aviv, saying he was reluctant to add another cook to the Middle East broth.

As if Israeli and U.S. reluctance were not a sufficient handicap, not all EU states share France's activism. Britain is keen to avoid offending the Americans and Germany has historical reasons for not crossing Israel.
A series of diplomatic incidents marred Chirac's visit to Israel but French and Israeli officials said they owed more to blunders on both sides than to deliberate ill-will.

The French leader upset many Israelis by first shunning their parliament, then making only a brief visit, while he was the first foreign leader to address the Palestinian Legislative Council, and also planned to speak in Jordan's legislature.

He also defied Israel by sending a junior minister to a disputed PLO office in East Jerusalem and having the PLO envoy to Paris, Leila Shahid, accompany him in the Old City after refusing a guided tour from the city's Israeli mayor.
Chirac hinted the EU might use economic pressure, noting that Israel's far-reaching 1995 association agreement with the 15-nation Union had yet to be ratified by member parliaments.
But Minerbi said the Israelis might not be bothered since they already have a huge trade deficit with Europe.
Nevertheless, the Israeli government did not entirely close the door to a European political role.
They are keen to pursue the Euro-Mediterranean dialogue launched last year, which was the first multilateral forum in which Israeli and Syrian ministers have met.

And diplomats say they are also aware that French and European ties to Syria and Iran could be useful in passing messages, controlling Hizbollah guerrillas in Lebanon and helping solve humanitarian issues such as missing Israeli soldiers.
